sections.title: Complete measures and completion
paragraphs: A measure space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mu)$ is complete if every subset $B$ of a measurable null set $A$ is measurable: $$B\subseteq A,\quad A\in\mathcal F,\quad\mu(A)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad B\in\mathcal F.$$ Monotonicity then gives $\mu(B)=0$. The notes record that uniform measure on a unit interval with only its Borel $\sigma$-algebra is not complete.

Given $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mu)$, let $$\mathcal N=\{N\subseteq\Omega:N\subseteq A\text{ for some }A\in\mathcal F\text{ with }\mu(A)=0\}.$$ Define $$\overline{\mathcal F}=\{A\mathbin{\triangle}N:A\in\mathcal F,\ N\in\mathcal N\},\qquad\overline\mu(A\mathbin{\triangle}N)=\mu(A).$$ Then $(\Omega,\overline{\mathcal F},\overline\mu)$ is a complete measure space. The small diagram depicts changing a measurable set only inside a null set.
editorial: The handwritten unit-interval example uses the endpoint convention $[0,1)$; the incompleteness is the same on $(0,1]$ or $[0,1]$. A null Cantor set contains non-Borel subsets, which are absent from the Borel $\sigma$-algebra but enter its completion.

The symmetric difference is $A\mathbin{\triangle}N=(A\setminus N)\cup(N\setminus A)$. The value of $\overline\mu$ is well defined: if two such representations agree, their measurable parts differ only within a measurable null set and therefore have the same measure. This symmetric-difference description is equivalent to adjoining arbitrary subsets of measurable null sets.

sections.title: Measurable maps and the generator test
paragraphs: Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$ and $(\Gamma,\mathcal G)$ be measurable spaces. A $(\Gamma,\mathcal G)$-valued random variable, or measurable map, is a function $X:\Omega\to\Gamma$ such that $$B\in\mathcal G\quad\Longrightarrow\quad X^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F.$$ A real random variable has target $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B_{\mathbb R})$; a random vector has target $(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B_{\mathbb R^n})$.
Generator test: if $\mathcal G=\sigma(\mathcal C)$ for a family $\mathcal C\subseteq2^\Gamma$, then $X$ is measurable if and only if $X^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F$ for every $B\in\mathcal C$.
proof: Let $$\widehat{\mathcal G}=\{B\in\sigma(\mathcal C):X^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F\}.$$ It contains $\varnothing$, since $X^{-1}(\varnothing)=\varnothing$.

If $B\in\widehat{\mathcal G}$, then $$X^{-1}(B^c)=\{\omega:X(\omega)\notin B\}=(X^{-1}(B))^c\in\mathcal F.$$ Hence $B^c\in\widehat{\mathcal G}$. Complements on the two sides are relative to $\Gamma$ and $\Omega$, respectively.

If $B_i\in\widehat{\mathcal G}$, then $$X^{-1}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}B_i\right)=\{\omega:X(\omega)\in\bigcup_iB_i\}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}X^{-1}(B_i)\in\mathcal F.$$ Thus $\widehat{\mathcal G}$ is a $\sigma$-algebra. It contains $\mathcal C$ by assumption, so it contains $\sigma(\mathcal C)$ and proves the test.

recall.question: Why can measurability be checked only on generators of the target sigma-algebra?
answer: The collection of target sets with measurable inverse image is itself a $\sigma$-algebra: inverse images preserve the empty set, complements, and countable unions. If this collection contains the generators, it contains the generated $\sigma$-algebra.
checks: Build a class of target sets, not source sets.
Use minimality of the generated sigma-algebra.

sections.title: Information generated by an observation
paragraphs: For a real function $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, the $\sigma$-algebra $\sigma(X)$ is the smallest $\sigma$-algebra on $\Omega$ making $X$ measurable. It is the intersection of all such $\sigma$-algebras, equivalently $$\sigma(X)=\sigma(\{X^{-1}(B):B\in\mathcal B_{\mathbb R}\}).$$ The same definition applies to a map into an arbitrary measurable target $(\Gamma,\mathcal G)$.

For any family of functions $\{X_\alpha\}_{\alpha\in S}$ on the same underlying space, $\sigma(X_\alpha:\alpha\in S)$ is the smallest $\sigma$-algebra making each member measurable. It is obtained by intersecting all $\sigma$-algebras with that property.

Example: let $\Omega=\mathbb R^2$ and $X(\omega_1,\omega_2)=\omega_1$. Then $$\sigma(X)=\{A\times\mathbb R:A\in\mathcal B_{\mathbb R}\}=\mathcal B_{\mathbb R}\otimes\mathcal F_0,$$ where $\mathcal F_0=\{\varnothing,\mathbb R\}$ is the trivial $\sigma$-algebra. The observation resolves first-coordinate Borel events and leaves the second coordinate unrestricted.
editorial: The preimage family $\{X^{-1}(B):B\in\mathcal G\}$ is already a $\sigma$-algebra, so the outer $\sigma$ in the displayed formula can be omitted. In the product notation, $\otimes$ means the $\sigma$-algebra generated by rectangles.

sections.title: Indicators and simple functions
paragraphs: For a measurable set $A$, its indicator is $$\mathbf1_A(\omega)=\begin{cases}1,&\omega\in A,\\0,&\omega\notin A.\end{cases}$$ A simple function is a finite linear combination $$X=\sum_{k=1}^{m}a_k\mathbf1_{A_k},\qquad a_k\in\mathbb R,\quad A_k\in\mathcal F,\quad m\in\mathbb N.$$ The notes denote their class by $\mathrm{SF}$.

Approximation theorem: every real measurable function $X$ has a sequence of measurable simple functions $X_n$ with $X_n(\omega)\to X(\omega)$ for every $\omega$. If $X\ge0$, the approximants can be chosen nonnegative and increasing: $X_n\le X_{n+1}\le X$.

sections.title: Building the simple approximations
paragraphs: For $X\ge0$, choose a mesh $\epsilon_n>0$ and an integer cutoff $L_n$. Set $$A_{k,n}=\{\omega:k\epsilon_n\le X(\omega)<(k+1)\epsilon_n\},\quad 0\le k<L_n,$$ and $$\widehat A_n=\{\omega:X(\omega)\ge L_n\epsilon_n\}.$$ Define $$X_n=\sum_{k=0}^{L_n-1}k\epsilon_n\mathbf1_{A_{k,n}}+L_n\epsilon_n\mathbf1_{\widehat A_n}.$$ The drawing partitions heights into horizontal bands and replaces each height by a lower grid value, with a top truncation level.

All sets used are measurable inverse images. If $\epsilon_n\downarrow0$ and $L_n\epsilon_n\uparrow\infty$, then $X_n\le X$. For a fixed $\omega$, eventually $L_n\epsilon_n>X(\omega)$, so $$X_n(\omega)\le X(\omega)<X_n(\omega)+\epsilon_n.$$ Therefore $|X(\omega)-X_n(\omega)|\to0$.

The notes choose $\epsilon_n=2^{-n}$ and express the lower approximation as the largest available grid value below $X(\omega)$: $$X_n(\omega)=\sup\{k\epsilon_n:k\epsilon_n\le X(\omega),\ 0\le k\le L_n,\ k\in\mathbb N\cup\{0\}\}.$$

For general real $X$, write $X=X_+-X_-$ with $X_+=\max(X,0)$ and $X_-=\max(-X,0)$. Approximate both nonnegative parts and set $$X_n=(X_+)_n-(X_-)_n.$$ Both terms are simple and converge pointwise, so their difference is a simple approximation to $X$. The notes check measurability of the positive part through threshold inverse images: for $a>0$, $\{X_+\ge a\}=\{X\ge a\}$; for $a\le0$, the set is $\Omega$.
editorial: The conditions $\epsilon_n\downarrow0$ and $L_n\epsilon_n\uparrow\infty$ ensure convergence but do not alone ensure $X_n\uparrow X$: the grids must also be nested. A concrete monotone choice is $\epsilon_n=2^{-n}$, $L_n=n2^n$, so the cap is $n$. Each old grid value remains available in the next grid and the cap increases. This supplies the condition implicit in the handwritten monotonicity claim.
The nonnegative approximants increase, while the signed approximants generally do not. Pointwise convergence is the conclusion for arbitrary signed $X$.

sections.title: The functional monotone class theorem
paragraphs: Let $\mathcal H$ be a collection of real-valued functions on $\Omega$ such that the constant function $1$ belongs to $\mathcal H$; $\mathcal H$ is a vector space over $\mathbb R$; and whenever $0\le h_n\in\mathcal H$ with $h_n\uparrow h$, for a real-valued $h$, the limit $h$ belongs to $\mathcal H$.

If $\mathcal P$ is a $\pi$-system and $\mathbf1_A\in\mathcal H$ for every $A\in\mathcal P$, then $\mathcal H$ contains every real-valued $\sigma(\mathcal P)$-measurable function. The notes also indicate the bounded version: if increasing-limit closure is required only when $h$ is bounded, the conclusion is for all bounded measurable functions.
proof: Define $$\mathcal L=\{A\subseteq\Omega:\mathbf1_A\in\mathcal H\}.$$ It contains $\mathcal P$ by hypothesis. Since $\mathbf1_\Omega=1\in\mathcal H$, it contains $\Omega$.
If $A\subseteq B$ and $A,B\in\mathcal L$, then $\mathbf1_{B\setminus A}=\mathbf1_B-\mathbf1_A\in\mathcal H$ by the vector-space property. Hence $B\setminus A\in\mathcal L$.

If $A_n\in\mathcal L$ and $A_n\uparrow A$, then $\mathbf1_{A_n}\uparrow\mathbf1_A$. Increasing-limit closure, even in the bounded version, gives $\mathbf1_A\in\mathcal H$. Thus $\mathcal L$ is a $\lambda$-system.

Dynkin’s theorem gives $\sigma(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal L$. Hence all indicators of sets in $\sigma(\mathcal P)$ lie in $\mathcal H$, and the vector-space property gives all their finite linear combinations, the simple functions.

Every nonnegative measurable function is an increasing limit of nonnegative simple functions, so belongs to $\mathcal H$ under the corresponding limit hypothesis. For a general real-valued function, take the difference of its positive and negative parts. For the bounded version, both parts and their approximants are bounded, so the same proof applies.

recall.question: In the functional monotone class theorem, how do you convert a class of functions into a class of sets, and then return to arbitrary measurable functions?
answer: Use $\mathcal L=\{A:\mathbf1_A\in\mathcal H\}$. The constant, vector-space, and monotone-limit assumptions make this a $\lambda$-system. Dynkin extends from $\mathcal P$ to $\sigma(\mathcal P)$. Linearity gives simple functions; increasing simple approximation gives nonnegative functions; subtraction gives signed functions.
checks: Match each function-space assumption to a set operation.

sections.title: Continuous maps, monotone maps, and composition
paragraphs: If $\Omega$ is topological and $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, then $f$ is Borel measurable: the inverse image of an open set is open, and open sets generate the Borel $\sigma$-algebra.
A monotone function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is Borel measurable. The notes suggest checking inverse images of intervals $(-\infty,a]$.
If $f:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(\Gamma,\mathcal G)$ and $g:(\Gamma,\mathcal G)\to(\Theta,\mathcal H)$ are measurable, then $g\circ f$ is measurable.

Example: if $X_1,X_2$ are real random variables on the same measurable space, then $f(\omega)=(X_1(\omega),X_2(\omega))$ is a random vector into $(\mathbb R^2,\mathcal B_{\mathbb R^2})$. For any continuous $g:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$, the function $g(X_1,X_2)=g\circ f$ is a real random variable.
proof: For $C\in\mathcal H$, $$ (g\circ f)^{-1}(C)=f^{-1}(g^{-1}(C)). $$ Measurability of $g$ puts $g^{-1}(C)$ in $\mathcal G$, then measurability of $f$ puts its inverse image in $\mathcal F$.
editorial: For a monotone real function, the inverse image of $(-\infty,a]$ is a ray, possibly open or closed at its finite endpoint, or is empty or all of $\mathbb R$. Each is Borel. For the vector example, inverse images of Borel rectangles are $X_1^{-1}(B_1)\cap X_2^{-1}(B_2)$, so the generator test proves vector measurability.

sections.title: Countable extrema and tail limits
paragraphs: For a sequence of random variables $X_n$ on the same measurable space, the lecture states that $$\inf_nX_n,\qquad\sup_nX_n,\qquad\liminf_{n\to\infty}X_n,\qquad\limsup_{n\to\infty}X_n$$ are measurable. The limit inferior is expressed using tail infima: $$Y_n=\inf_{m\ge n}X_m,\qquad\liminf_nX_n=\sup_nY_n.$$
proof: The handwritten argument starts by testing a threshold inverse image for $X=\inf_nX_n$ and rewriting it as a countable union of threshold events for the $X_n$. The valid strict-threshold identity is $$\{\inf_nX_n<b\}=\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty}\{X_n<b\}\in\mathcal F.$$ This proves measurability of the infimum using generators of the extended-real Borel $\sigma$-algebra.

Negation gives $\sup_nX_n=-\inf_n(-X_n)$. Apply the infimum result to each tail to see that $Y_n=\inf_{m\ge n}X_m$ is measurable. Then $\sup_nY_n$ is measurable. Similarly, $$\limsup_nX_n=\inf_n\sup_{m\ge n}X_m$$ is measurable.
editorial: The notes write a non-strict threshold identity $\{\inf_nX_n\le b\}=\bigcup_n\{X_n\le b\}$, which fails if the infimum is not attained. For example, $X_n=1/n$ and $b=0$ make the left side all of $\Omega$ and the right side empty. The proof above corrects the signs to strict inequalities.

Even if every $X_n$ is finite, the displayed extrema and tail limits can be infinite. They are therefore extended-real-valued measurable functions in general; they are real random variables only when their values are finite. The additional supremum and tail-limit steps above expand the reduction indicated in the handwritten proof.

recall.question: Prove that a countable infimum is measurable. Which threshold inequality avoids the unattained-infimum problem?
answer: For each real $b$, use $\{\inf_nX_n<b\}=\bigcup_n\{X_n<b\}$. Countable union closure gives measurability. Replacing both strict signs by non-strict signs is invalid, as the sequence $X_n=1/n$ at threshold zero demonstrates.
